stem: A Driftlight analyst drags the dimension `Plan` onto Color on the Marks card. What does Tableau display?

options.text: A continuous range of colours with a start value and an end value in the legend
options.rationale: This quantitative legend is what a continuous field (typically a measure) gets, not a dimension.

options.text: One colour for every plan, with the opacity of the marks changing by plan
options.rationale: Opacity is a separate formatting setting; a dimension on Color assigns distinct colours.

options.text: A categorical palette, with a distinct colour and a legend entry for each plan
options.rationale: A discrete field on Color gets a categorical palette, one colour per member, plus a legend.

options.text: A single legend entry named Plan, with all the marks in the default blue
options.rationale: Encoding with a field splits the marks by colour; they do not all stay blue.

explanation: Dropping a field on Color encodes it. A discrete field (typically a dimension) gets a categorical palette with one colour per member, and Tableau adds a legend that lists them.

stem: What kind of legend does Tableau show when `AVG(Monthly Price)` is placed on Color?

options.text: A quantitative legend with a continuous range of colours
options.rationale: A continuous field (typically a measure) on Color gets a gradient legend.

options.text: A categorical legend with one swatch for each distinct price
options.rationale: Categorical palettes belong to discrete fields; this aggregated measure is continuous.

options.text: No legend, because a measure can only be used to format all marks equally
options.rationale: Any field on Color is an encoding and creates a legend, whatever its type.

options.text: A stepped legend with ten fixed bins that cannot be changed
options.rationale: Stepped Color is an optional setting in Edit Colors; the default is a continuous range.

explanation: The palette follows the continuity of the field on Color. Discrete fields get distinct colours; continuous fields get a gradient and a quantitative legend.

stem: The analyst wants every mark on a sheet to be orange, with no legend and no change to what the view shows. What should they do?

options.text: Drag `Plan` to Color and assign orange to each member in Edit Colors
options.rationale: This encodes a field, which adds a legend and splits the marks by member.

options.text: Choose Format > Font and set the colour of the pane text to orange
options.rationale: Format > Font changes text in the pane and headers, not the colour of marks.

options.text: Choose Format > Workbook and set a workbook-wide mark colour
options.rationale: The Format Workbook pane sets fonts, not the colour of the marks on a sheet.

options.text: Click Color on the Marks card and pick orange from the menu
options.rationale: Clicking Color without dropping a field formats every mark and adds no legend.

explanation: Clicking Color on the Marks card without dropping a field is formatting: it recolours every mark the same way. Dropping a field is encoding and always creates a legend.

stem: The analyst wants to choose a different palette for the field currently on Color. Which path on the Marks card opens the right dialog?

options.text: Shape > Edit Shape
options.rationale: Edit Shape changes the shapes of marks, not their colours.

options.text: Color > Edit Colors
options.rationale: Edit Colors is where you pick a colour or assign a palette; the colour legend menu offers the same command.

options.text: Size > Edit Sizes
options.rationale: Edit Sizes controls how mark sizes vary, not their colours.

options.text: Label > Edit Colors
options.rationale: Label controls text on the marks; the palette dialog is reached through Color.

explanation: On the Marks card, click Color and then Edit Colors, or use Edit Colors from the colour legend menu. For a discrete field you can pick a colour per member or assign a palette.

stem: A continuous field is on Color. Which Edit Colors setting groups its values into uniform bins instead of a smooth gradient?

options.text: Reversed
options.rationale: Reversed inverts the colours of the palette; it does not create bins.

options.text: Stepped Color
options.rationale: Stepped Color divides the values into uniform bins, each with its own colour.

options.text: Use Full Color Range
options.rationale: This stretches a diverging palette across the full range; it does not bin the values.

options.text: Assign Palette
options.rationale: Assign Palette applies a palette to the members of a discrete field.

explanation: For a continuous field you can choose a sequential or diverging palette. Stepped Color groups the values into uniform bins, and Reversed inverts the colours.

stem: Before the analyst changes anything, how does Tableau draw most marks and the text marks of a new view?

options.text: Most marks in grey, text in black, and all marks with a thin dark border
options.rationale: The default colour of most marks is blue, and by default there is no border.

options.text: Most marks in blue, text in blue, and all marks with a white halo
options.rationale: Text is black by default, and halos only apply with a background image or a map.

options.text: Most marks in orange, text in grey, and all marks without a border
options.rationale: Orange is not the default colour; most marks start out blue and text black.

options.text: Most marks in blue, text in black, and all marks without a border
options.rationale: Blue is the default colour for most marks, black for text, and marks have no border by default.

explanation: Every mark has a default colour: blue for most marks and black for text. By default Tableau draws marks without a border, so borders are a format you switch on.

stem: Which actions encode data on the Marks card and create a legend? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Dragging `Genre` onto Color
options.rationale: A field on Color is an encoding with a categorical palette and a legend.

options.text: Clicking Color and choosing a red from the menu
options.rationale: This formats every mark the same way; no field is involved and no legend appears.

options.text: Dragging `SUM(Minutes Watched)` onto Color
options.rationale: A measure on Color is an encoding too, with a quantitative legend.

options.text: Clicking Color and moving the Opacity slider
options.rationale: Opacity is formatting for all marks and adds no legend.

options.text: Clicking Color and switching on mark borders
options.rationale: Borders are formatting; they do not depend on a field.

explanation: Encoding means dropping a field on Color, which adds information and a legend. Clicking Color without a field only changes how all marks look.

stem: Which statements about colour palettes in Edit Colors are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A diverging palette can be chosen for a continuous field.
options.rationale: Diverging palettes are offered for continuous fields.

options.text: A discrete field on Color uses a sequential gradient by default.
options.rationale: A discrete field gets a categorical palette with one colour per member.

options.text: Stepped Color is available for a continuous field.
options.rationale: Stepped Color groups the values of a continuous field into uniform bins.

options.text: Use Full Color Range works with every palette of a discrete field.
options.rationale: It applies to a diverging palette on a continuous field, not to discrete members.

options.text: Tableau 10 is an ordinal palette listed at the bottom.
options.rationale: Categorical palettes such as Tableau 10 are at the top; ordinal ones such as Orange are at the bottom.

explanation: The palette follows the continuity of the field. Continuous colour has sequential and diverging palettes plus Stepped Color; discrete colour has categorical palettes.

stem: Which settings can the analyst change after clicking Color on the Marks card, without dropping any field? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Opacity of all marks
options.rationale: The Color menu sets opacity for every mark.

options.text: Stepped Color
options.rationale: Stepped Color needs a continuous field on Color.

options.text: Borders around the marks
options.rationale: By default marks have no border; the Color menu can add one.

options.text: Reversed
options.rationale: Reversing a palette needs a field on Color.

options.text: Assign Palette
options.rationale: Assigning a palette needs the members of a discrete field on Color.

explanation: The Color menu formats every mark: its colour, opacity and borders. The palette options in Edit Colors only make sense once a field is on Color.

stem: Which statements about the default look of marks are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: For most marks, blue is the default colour.
options.rationale: Most marks start out blue.

options.text: Most marks are grey until a field is placed on Color.
options.rationale: The default colour is blue, not grey.

options.text: Text marks are black by default.
options.rationale: Black is the default colour for text.

options.text: Text marks are blue by default.
options.rationale: Blue is the default for most marks, but text is black.

options.text: Marks are drawn with a thin white border by default.
options.rationale: By default Tableau displays all marks without a border.

explanation: Marks start with a default colour: blue for most marks and black for text. Without a border, they only change when you format them or encode a field on Color.

stem: The analyst wants one font for every title, label and header in the whole workbook. Which menu path should they use?

options.text: Format > Workbook
options.rationale: The Format Workbook pane changes all font settings in a workbook.

options.text: Format > Font
options.rationale: Format > Font formats the pane and header text of the current sheet only.

options.text: Format > Borders
options.rationale: Borders are a part of the view to format on one sheet, and not a font setting.

options.text: Format > Animations
options.rationale: Animations control transitions between views, not fonts.

explanation: Format > Workbook opens the Format Workbook pane, where one change reaches all font settings in the workbook, including titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards.

stem: The analyst chooses Format > Workbook. What changes in the Tableau window?

options.text: A dialog opens over the view and blocks the sheet until it is closed
options.rationale: Workbook formatting happens in a pane, not in a modal dialog.

options.text: A new tab named Workbook appears on the Marks card
options.rationale: The Marks card is not involved; the pane sits where the Data pane was.

options.text: The Format Workbook pane replaces the Data pane
options.rationale: The pane takes the place of the Data pane while it is open.

options.text: The Data pane stays and a font list is added below the Filters shelf
options.rationale: The Format Workbook pane replaces the Data pane instead of sitting beside it.

explanation: Opening Format > Workbook shows a pane in place of the Data pane. From there you change all font settings of the workbook, as well as the titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards.

stem: The analyst made a sheet-level change to a header font. Later a colleague changes the font under Format > Workbook. What happens to the sheet-level change?

options.text: It is kept, because sheet-level formatting always wins
options.rationale: Workbook-level font changes overwrite sheet-level ones, not the other way around.

options.text: It is kept for headers but overwritten for pane text
options.rationale: Tableau does not split sheet-level font changes this way; they are overwritten.

options.text: Tableau asks which of the two fonts to keep for every sheet
options.rationale: There is no such prompt; the workbook setting simply takes over.

options.text: It is overwritten by the new workbook font
options.rationale: Changing the workbook font overwrites font changes made at sheet level.

explanation: Workbook formatting is the broadest scope. Applying a font there overwrites font changes made on individual sheets, so set the workbook font first and make exceptions afterwards.

stem: After setting several fonts in the Format Workbook pane, the analyst wants to undo all of it. Which command does that?

options.text: Reset All Sheets
options.rationale: Reset All Sheets belongs to Animations and returns sheets to the workbook default.

options.text: Reset to Defaults
options.rationale: Reset to Defaults in the Format Workbook pane undoes the workbook changes.

options.text: Clear Sheet
options.rationale: Clear Sheet empties the current view; it does not touch workbook formatting.

options.text: Assign Palette
options.rationale: Assign Palette is for colours of a discrete field, not for fonts.

explanation: The Format Workbook pane has a Reset to Defaults command that returns the formatting to Tableau's defaults.

stem: What does Format > Font apply to?

options.text: The pane text or the header text, or both, of the current view
options.rationale: Format > Font works on the view of the current sheet, for either pane or header text.

options.text: Every sheet, dashboard and story title in the workbook
options.rationale: That is the reach of Format > Workbook, not of Format > Font.

options.text: Only the text on the Marks card Label property
options.rationale: Format > Font formats the pane and header text of the view, not only labels.

options.text: Only the titles of stories and dashboards
options.rationale: Titles of stories and dashboards are handled in the Format Workbook pane.

explanation: Format > Font is sheet-level formatting. For one view you can set the font, style, size and colour of the pane text, the header text or both.

stem: The head of design wants a consistent look in a workbook, with a few exceptions on individual sheets. What is the best order of work?

options.text: Format each sheet first, then apply the font under Format > Workbook
options.rationale: The workbook font would overwrite every sheet-level change made earlier.

options.text: Use Format > Workbook for the exceptions and Format > Font for the baseline
options.rationale: This reverses the scopes: workbook is broad and sheet-level is specific.

options.text: Set the workbook font first, then override the exceptions on those sheets
options.rationale: The workbook setting is the baseline; later sheet-level changes stay.

options.text: Set a font on every sheet separately and never open Format > Workbook
options.rationale: This works but is slow, and misses titles of stories and dashboards that the workbook pane covers.

explanation: Start broad, then refine. The workbook font gives every sheet the same base look, and the sheet-level exceptions come after it so they are not overwritten.

stem: Which items can be changed in the Format Workbook pane? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: All font settings in the workbook
options.rationale: The pane changes all font settings in a workbook.

options.text: The join type between two tables
options.rationale: Joins are set in the data source, not in the Format pane.

options.text: The font settings for titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards
options.rationale: Titles of these are covered by the Format Workbook pane.

options.text: The data type of every dimension
options.rationale: Data types are changed in the Data pane or data source, not by formatting.

options.text: The default aggregation of every measure
options.rationale: Default properties are not set in the Format Workbook pane.

explanation: The Format Workbook pane is for appearance: all fonts in the workbook, plus the titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards.

stem: For a view formatted with Format > Font, which properties can the analyst specify for pane text or header text? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: The font
options.rationale: Font is one of the properties you can specify.

options.text: The sort order of the members
options.rationale: Sorting is not a font property.

options.text: The size
options.rationale: Size is one of the properties you can specify.

options.text: The data source connection
options.rationale: Connections are not part of text formatting.

options.text: The colour
options.rationale: Colour is one of the properties you can specify.

options.text: The aggregation of the measure
options.rationale: Aggregation is a pill setting, not a font property.

explanation: For a view you can set font, style, size and colour for the pane text, the header text or both.

stem: Which statements about workbook-level and sheet-level fonts are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Format > Workbook can overwrite font changes made on individual sheets.
options.rationale: The workbook setting takes over, including sheet-level changes.

options.text: Format > Font changes the font of every sheet in the workbook.
options.rationale: Format > Font only reaches the current sheet.

options.text: Format > Font changes only the pane and header text of the current sheet.
options.rationale: It works at the worksheet level.

options.text: Format > Workbook only works on dashboards.
options.rationale: It covers all font settings in the workbook, sheets included.

options.text: Reset to Defaults only works for one sheet at a time.
options.rationale: It belongs to the Format Workbook pane and resets workbook formatting.

explanation: Workbook is the broad scope and the worksheet is the narrow one. A workbook change reaches every sheet and can overwrite sheet-level fonts; Format > Font stays on one sheet.

stem: Which mark type must be selected on the Marks card for the shapes assigned to a field to show?

options.text: Circle
options.rationale: Circle marks are drawn as circles whatever is on the Shape property.

options.text: Square
options.rationale: Square marks are drawn as squares and ignore the shapes.

options.text: Shape
options.rationale: Shapes only appear when the mark type is Shape.

options.text: Text
options.rationale: Text marks show words; they do not draw shapes.

explanation: Set the mark type to Shape, then drag a field to Shape on the Marks card. Tableau then draws a different shape for each member.

stem: What does Tableau do when the dimension `Device` is placed on Shape?

options.text: It separates the marks by member and assigns a unique shape to each
options.rationale: A dimension on Shape splits the marks by member, with a shape per member.

options.text: It converts `Device` to a measure and uses one shape for all marks
options.rationale: Only a measure is converted (to a discrete measure); a dimension is kept.

options.text: It keeps one mark per row and varies only the size of the shapes
options.rationale: Size is a separate property; Shape assigns a different shape per member.

options.text: It uses one shape but adds a legend with the names of the members
options.rationale: Each member gets its own shape, which is what the legend shows.

explanation: Placing a dimension on Shape splits the marks according to its members and gives each member a shape. The legend lists which shape stands for which member.

stem: Which view makes the Automatic mark type pick Shape?

options.text: A continuous date on Columns and a measure on Rows
options.rationale: This combination is drawn as a line.

options.text: A measure as the innermost field on Rows and another measure on Columns
options.rationale: Automatic uses Shape when measures are the innermost fields on both shelves.

options.text: A dimension on Columns and a measure on Rows
options.rationale: A dimension with a measure is drawn as bars.

options.text: A dimension on Columns and another dimension on Rows
options.rationale: Only dimensions with no continuous field gives text.

explanation: When measures are the innermost fields on both Rows and Columns, Automatic picks the Shape mark. You can also set the mark type to Shape yourself.

stem: A dimension with 14 members is placed on Shape and the default shapes are used. What happens?

options.text: Tableau shows a message and refuses to draw more than ten members
options.rationale: There is no such limit on members; the default shapes repeat.

options.text: The extra four members are drawn as plain circles without a shape
options.rationale: The shapes repeat; the remaining members do not turn into circles.

options.text: The four smallest members are grouped into one member called Other
options.rationale: Tableau does not group members automatically.

options.text: Ten unique shapes are used, and the shapes repeat for the remaining members
options.rationale: By default, ten unique shapes are used to encode dimensions, then they repeat.

explanation: The default shape palette has ten shapes. With more than ten members they repeat, so two members can share a shape; assign shapes by hand or filter to avoid that.

stem: Which command on the shape legend's card menu opens the dialog for choosing other shapes?

options.text: Edit Shape
options.rationale: Edit Shape (or clicking Shape on the Marks card) lets you pick shapes from palettes.

options.text: Edit Colors
options.rationale: Edit Colors changes the palette of the Color property.

options.text: Edit Sizes
options.rationale: Edit Sizes changes how sizes vary on the Size property.

options.text: Reload Shapes
options.rationale: Reload Shapes refreshes the custom shape palettes from the repository after a change.

explanation: You can click Shape on the Marks card, or use Edit Shape on the legend's menu. There you choose from palettes such as filled shapes, arrows and weather symbols.

stem: The analyst has a set of PNG image files that should become a custom shape palette. Where do they go?

options.text: In a new folder inside My Tableau Repository\Datasources
options.rationale: Datasources holds connection files, not shape palettes.

options.text: In a new folder inside My Tableau Repository\Workbooks
options.rationale: Workbooks holds workbook files; Tableau reads shapes from the Shapes folder.

options.text: In a new folder inside My Tableau Repository\Shapes
options.rationale: The folder name becomes the name of the palette.

options.text: In the same folder as the workbook that will use them
options.rationale: Tableau reads custom shapes from the repository, not from beside the workbook.

explanation: Copy the image files into a new folder in My Tableau Repository\Shapes. The folder name becomes the palette name and shows up in the Edit Shape dialog.

stem: Tableau was running when the analyst copied a new folder of images into the Shapes folder. The palette is missing in Edit Shape. What should they do?

options.text: Click Assign Palette in the Edit Colors dialog
options.rationale: Assign Palette is about colour, not shapes.

options.text: Click Reload Shapes in the Edit Shape dialog
options.rationale: Reload Shapes loads the new palette without restarting.

options.text: Choose Data > Refresh All Extracts
options.rationale: Extract refreshes update data, not shape palettes.

options.text: Drag a measure onto Shape on the Marks card
options.rationale: This would convert the measure to discrete but not load new images.

explanation: If Tableau was already running, use Reload Shapes in the Edit Shape dialog so that the new palette appears.

stem: Which image file formats can be used for custom shapes? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: .gif
options.rationale: GIF is listed as supported.

options.text: .xlsx
options.rationale: A spreadsheet is not an image format.

options.text: .bmp
options.rationale: BMP is listed as supported.

options.text: .pdf
options.rationale: PDF is not among the formats for custom shapes.

options.text: .tiff
options.rationale: TIFF is listed as supported.

options.text: .csv
options.rationale: A text data file is not an image.

explanation: Custom shapes are image files: .png, .gif, .jpg, .bmp or .tiff, copied into a folder in My Tableau Repository\Shapes.

stem: Which statements about fields on Shape are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A dimension on Shape gets a unique shape per member.
options.rationale: Marks are separated by the members of the dimension.

options.text: A measure on Shape stays continuous and gets a gradient.
options.rationale: A measure on Shape is converted to a discrete measure.

options.text: A measure on Shape is converted to a discrete measure.
options.rationale: Shape needs discrete values, so the measure is converted.

options.text: A dimension on Shape adds no legend.
options.rationale: A field on Shape is an encoding and adds a legend.

options.text: Shapes never repeat, however many members there are.
options.rationale: By default ten shapes are used and they repeat after that.

explanation: Shape is a discrete encoding: dimensions get one shape per member, and a measure is turned into a discrete measure first.
